newsitem.title: USA: Motorola plans $12.9 bln satellite system.
newsitem.headline: Motorola plans $12.9 bln satellite system.

text.p: Motorola Inc said on Tuesday it plans to build a third satellite communications system estimated to cost some $12.9 billion.

Motorola said it has asked the Federal Communications Commission for authorization to build Celestri, a 63-satellite system to provide multimedia, voice, data and video services to residential users, small businesses, multinational corporations and even telecommunications service providers anywhere in the world.
Motorola spokesman Robert Edwards said the company hopes to begin providing service in the year 2002.
"In order to meet that time table, we would have to begin launching (satellites) sometime at the end of 2000 or the beginning of 2001," Edwards said.
Motorola said it is currently seeking additional investors for the systems, including other companies and banks.
Celestri will use both low-orbit satellites which circle about 900 miles above the Earth and geosynchronous Earth orbit satellites which are fixed some 22,300 miles above the Earth.

Motorola pioneered and owns about a 25 percent stake in Iridium LLC, which has already launched five of the 66 satellites planned for that estimated $3.4 billion network, and is scheduled to launch an another seven on Wednesday.
Iridium, which includes Iridium World Communications Ltd and various other companies, plans to provide telecommunications services on wireless phones and pagers to anywhere in the world.

Schaumburg, Ill.-based Motorola is also planning M-Star for high-speed, high-volume data transfer. At least some of the technology used in M-Star will be embedded in the Celestri system, Motorola said.
Despite the high price tag on the Celestri system, Motorola said the cost to the consumer will be relatively cheap and based on usage.
For residential users, for example, Edwards said the company is developing a $750 home unit about two feet in diameter which attaches to the roof.

"While the cost of constructing the Celestri LEO (low-Earth orbit) System will be high in absolute terms, the system's global reach makes it possible to spread that cost over a large number of potential users, resulting in a fraction of the per-user cost that would be incurred to build out a terrestrial broadband network, whether nationwide or worldwide," the company said in a summary of the FCC filing.
Celestri will transmit data, such as a connection to the Internet, at speeds ranging from 64 kilobits per second to 155 megabits per second.

Each Celestri satellite will include an intelligent switching sytem and will link with the current wire and fiber optic telecommunications systems on the ground. The satellites will weigh about 7,000 pounds each.
